entries.source_text: We start with the observation that aging gerontologists often engage in two distinct discourses on aging—one public and one private. This separation entails “othering,” which reproduces agism and stigma. Based on personal experience, insight from colleagues and writers, and concepts from symbolic interaction perspectives, we argue that becoming old to some degree involves becoming a stranger. Before reaching old age, both of us have been in the position of strangers due to social experiences that left us “off the line” or “on the margins.” Examples are crossing social borders related to nations, class structures, gender, race, health status, and generations. Our stories illustrate how aging is more than personal. It is interpersonal—shaped by social history, policies, interdependence in relationships, and the precariousness of old age. Such phenomena often show sharp contrasts in the interpersonal worlds and social experiences of women and men. Reflecting on our own journeys as life course migrants leaves us acutely aware of both the social problems and potential promises of aging.

entries.source_text: Today’s gerontologists often carry on two distinct discourses about aging: one public and scientific; the other private and personal. These discussions are typically at odds. The public voice lauds active aging; the private one secretly confesses limitations and precariousness. At professional meetings, we have also observed pervasive “othering,” as even the most senior gerontologists refer to old people as “they,” not “we.” Reflections about personal aging constitute, literally, another story. This pattern reproduces agism and stigma. Separating private and public discourses may seriously limit insights, both about processes of aging and the societies in which we live.

entries.source_text: Hendricks cites Schütz, who wrote extensively on the concept of meaning, which is also central in our framework. We see personal meaning as interpersonal. A sense of self is created and maintained through social mirrors, in webs of interdependent lives that span family generations and historical time. As societies change, so do socially constructed meanings. Consequently, the older individuals get, the more likely it is that they have core meanings that are not shared by many people around them, and they have few witnesses who know where they have been. To some extent, then, they become strangers to other people and even to themselves.

entries.source_text: In exploring the territory of old age, we draw from the “Chicago School” of sociology, especially the symbolic interaction perspective. It offers insights into how humans create and maintain a sense of self and continuity across social borders—including phases of life, cultures, and social structures. entries.source_text: Two classical pieces help us understand our border crossings: Simmel’s (1908) and Schütz’s (1944) essays on The Stranger. Both authors crossed borders between nations, disciplines, and professions. For Simmel, the stranger experiences a “unity of nearness and remoteness,” as well as “freedom” gained from a combination of “indifference and involvement.” Schütz pointed to the stranger’s ability to challenge a “tested system of recipes.” A stranger will ask “How?” and “Why?” about phenomena natives take as given. Our personal stories will illustrate how we have been in the position of the stranger before old age. These experiences make us challenge some common “recipes” in contemporary gerontology.

entries.source_text: To us, a central aspect of understanding aging as interpersonal is that the older we are, the more likely it is that we have experienced the pain of losing longstanding relationships with others who constitute the “library of our lives.” Some authors use the terms “consociates” (Plath, 1980) or “co-biographers” for such others (Bertaux, 1981). Kahn and Antonucci (1980) discuss convoys of support. Recently, G. O. Hagestad had the painful realization that her 92-year-old aunt is the sole person who has known her since she was born. Those of us who are life course migrants have difficulties finding co-biographers when it is time to compose a life history. As Erikson (1986) claimed, the key developmental task in old age is to find integrity—threads of continuity in one’s life history. Butler (1963) called it life review. Experienced clinicians report that they are increasingly asked to help individuals compose a “good ending.” The two of us have only started writing our histories, but work on this essay has accelerated the process!

entries.source_text: The oldest of three siblings and a “war child,” I started life in occupied Norway and grew up in a nation trying to rebuild in times of scarcity. My mother came from a coastal community. Bertha’s early life, which started in 1915, was marked by losses and uncertainty: her mother gave birth to nine children, four of whom died before school age. An uncle and two cousins perished at sea in a fishing boat; neighbors died in the big flu pandemic. Bertha came to see normal life as unpredictable and precarious. She never made plans without adding: “if we live.” After marriage, her life exemplifies a phenomenon described by Elder (1974): Following massive uncertainty in the Great Depression, women found traditional female domesticity to be a safe harbor in adulthood. She shared with me the meanings of a warm and safe home, with flowers, candles, and the smell of home-baked bread. Although she never expected a long life, she lived past 80. I still think of her when I light candles, which I do all year, and when I invite guests to sit at a nicely decorated table and enjoy good food.

entries.source_text: My father Tönnes, born in 1908, was the oldest of nine siblings, all of whom survived to adulthood. The small inland farm provided safety and the land provided food. His mother created healthy meals based on raw materials from farm and forest. For me, she continues to be the model of serenity, strength, and an ability to lose herself in silly giggles. Tönnes gave up his right to the farm in order to become a teacher. He saw teaching as a calling and loved his work. I, too, have loved teaching, treasuring the freedom academic work gives us to keep our inner, curious 4 year old. My father took his three children hiking and skiing in the mountains, teaching us to notice plants and animals. In retirement, he continued to be active and curious, seeking out contact with young people. When physical decline limited his options for engagement, he disengaged. Like Job, he was “full of days.” For those of us whose lives were interwoven with his, it was hard to accept his personal aging choice. But for me, my children and grandchildren, he left a legacy of curiosity about the world around us, combined with love and respect for nature. A close connection with untouched nature will always be at the core of my sense of self, providing continuity and peace. And through significant others in two generations above me, I learned to value joys that do not cost money.

entries.source_text: Most of my childhood, we lived in a rural schoolhouse that bore marks left by occupying military troops. Our cohort location left permanent marks on our bodies and values. Nutrition was limited in years of rationing. Many members of my cohort have poor teeth and muscle-skeletal problems. We did not have inoculations against common childhood diseases, nor antibiotics. A close cousin died of polio. Given childhood experiences, I have difficulties throwing things out, be it leftover food or used clothing. Because family solidarity was crucial in hard times, kin ties are important to me. We have an annual family reunion at the family farm, where my brother now lives.

entries.source_text: My cohort location also brought opportunities my parents did not have. As new policies increased access to universities, I became part of an educational vanguard and had many experiences of being “the first” or “the only.” I was the only PhD student in my cohort who had children. Starting a position at Penn State in the late 1970s, I was the only woman faculty member in my unit who was a mother. In early phases of my career, I was often the only woman in the room during national and international meetings. Such experiences taught me how being a statistical outlier makes it difficult to build a convoy of peer support—both in professional and family roles. However, I was fortunate to have two women mentors and role models: philosopher May Brodbeck in graduate school and colleague Bernice Neugarten in my first academic job. Early career years form a stark contrast to life after 70 years of age, which has brought a sense of being invisible, and being called “sweetie” and “honey” in the United States!

entries.source_text: A sense of being a lone traveler was at its strongest when I was diagnosed with stage IV breast cancer in 1993, shortly after my 50th birthday. Before turning 51, I had surgery, chemotherapy and radiation. After treatments, I developed life-threatening infections. In those critical 2 years, the possibility of death was very real. The hardest part of facing death was linked to interdependence and scripts of normal, expectable lives. I felt that my two daughters were too young to become motherless, and I had an intense hope to see them become mothers and me a grandmother. My mother was extremely shaken, saying, “I can’t outlive one of my children!”

entries.source_text: The illness and its aftermath brought back issues raised in my philosophy courses, especially Feigl’s (1967) discussion of mind/body dualism. I kept thinking “if this is my body, where am I supposed to go?” Later, I realized that I had a preview of old age: experiencing premature precariousness. This was not only a personal crisis but also an interpersonal one. Consociates could not understand that I was unable to fully participate in everyday life. I wanted to say: I am not unreliable; my body is! American and Norwegian cultures both emphasize “attitude is key! Pull yourself together!” Many proponents of “active aging” start from such premises, which may entail problematic dichotomous thinking: active/passive, independent/dependent, and able/disabled. Once labeled ill, disabled or dependent on help, you often lose the opportunity to use the capacity—albeit limited—that you still have. In nursing homes, residents are often blocked from participating in activities they could master.

entries.source_text: The illness made me fall out of time (Hagestad, 1996), creating dramatic insights into how adult roles are built on assumptions about a healthy body, predictable linear time, and expected durations. When I no longer conformed to normal timetable scripts, people were hesitant to include me in plans. Part of this reluctance was due to stigma. Cancer scares people, and many feel a need to “other” the patient. The role of patient overshadowed all others that were at the core of my sense of self: mother, sister, daughter, friend, and professor.

entries.source_text: Like many cancer patients, I experienced reorganized convoys: central persons disappeared; peripheral individuals moved to the center. In this process, I became very close to my sister, who knows a great deal about being a patient. Growing up, we did not really know each other, since she is 8 years my junior. Before reaching adulthood, she was diagnosed with a rare autoimmune syndrome, which has created a number of near-death situations. On many of those occasions, we were on different sides of the Atlantic. During my illness, she became a crucial support person. My brother, who is a medical doctor, also provided lifesaving insight and help. When we recently celebrated his 70th birthday, we sisters said that without him, neither of us would have lived to experience the party. Supportive others can make an enormous difference in reducing discontinuity, even death. If a colleague had not nominated me to give the opening address for the UN International Year of Older Persons (Hagestad, 1998), an honor that provided visibility, I may not have been able to resume academic work.

entries.source_text: Since my illness, I respond like my mother when plans are being made: “if I live.” Often, the response is “don’t say that!” Reactions illustrate Blythe’s (1979) statement: “we place dying in what we take to be its logical position, which is at the close of a long life—when our ancestors accepted the futility of placing it in any position at all” (p. 12). Fellow gerontologist Hendricks, also a cancer survivor in his 70s, reports similar reactions. Both of us feel out of step with cohort peers and sense a denial of finitude. I wonder if our illness experiences make it easier for Joe and me to be old, because we have faced premature precariousness. We have both also “gone public” with personal accounts of cancer, trying to reduce stigma. My body carries scars and damage left by a bombardment of broad-spectrum cancer treatment which, in my 70s, join forces with “normal aging,” such as loss of bone mass and muscle strength. Because of my illness two decades ago, I may be more ready than many peers to accept old age, also when it brings pain and reduced energy. Brody (2010) writes humorously about her own aging: “I don’t remember becoming old.” Personally, I do remember the day that I became old—or incorporated old age in my sense of self. I was in my 60s, going through security at an airport. An officer called out, “The shoes on the belt belong to the old lady!” Looking around, I saw no old woman. The looking glass was there, and the self got the message! Since then, the list of things I can no longer do has gotten longer. I doubt that I will ever ski again, at least down hills, and I have climbed my last mountain. But I have a daily regiment of exercise and (short!) walks in the woods; I still love gardening (in a garden that has shrunk). I am retired, but people call me “still active.” We academics are lucky in that we can to some degree “keep on working” as long as we can think. I am fortunate to still be invited to give occasional keynotes and informal presentations in several countries, and I still write!

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 내 몸에는 광범위 암치료의 집중 공세가 남긴 흉터와 손상이 있으며, 이는 내가 70대가 되자 골량과 근력의 감소 같은 “정상적 노화”와 힘을 합친다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: My body carries scars and damage left by a bombardment of broad-spectrum cancer treatment which, in my 70s, join forces with “normal aging,” such as loss of bone mass and muscle strength.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 20년 전의 질병 때문에 나는 고통과 에너지 저하가 따르는 노년도 많은 또래보다 더 잘 받아들일 준비가 되어 있을지 모른다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: Because of my illness two decades ago, I may be more ready than many peers to accept old age, also when it brings pain and reduced energy.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: Brody(2010)는 자신의 노화에 관해 “나는 언제 늙었는지 기억나지 않는다”고 유머러스하게 썼다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: Brody (2010) writes humorously about her own aging: “I don’t remember becoming old.”

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 개인적으로 나는 내가 늙은 사람이 된 날, 즉 자아감 속에 노년을 통합한 날을 기억한다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: Personally, I do remember the day that I became old—or incorporated old age in my sense of self.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 60대에 공항 보안검색대를 지나고 있었다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: I was in my 60s, going through security at an airport.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 한 직원이 “벨트 위의 신발은 저 할머니 거예요!”라고 외쳤다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: An officer called out, “The shoes on the belt belong to the old lady!”

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 둘러보았지만 늙은 여성은 보이지 않았다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: Looking around, I saw no old woman.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 거울은 그곳에 있었고, 자아는 그 메시지를 받아들였다!
sentence_pairs.source_text: The looking glass was there, and the self got the message!

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 그 뒤로 더 이상 할 수 없는 일들의 목록은 길어졌다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: Since then, the list of things I can no longer do has gotten longer.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 적어도 비탈을 내려오는 스키는 다시는 타지 못할 것 같고, 마지막 등산도 이미 끝났다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: I doubt that I will ever ski again, at least down hills, and I have climbed my last mountain.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 하지만 나는 매일 정해진 운동과 숲속의 (짧은!) 산책을 하고, 여전히 정원 가꾸기를 좋아한다(정원은 작아졌지만).
sentence_pairs.source_text: But I have a daily regiment of exercise and (short!) walks in the woods; I still love gardening (in a garden that has shrunk).

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 나는 은퇴했지만 사람들은 나를 “여전히 활동적”이라고 부른다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: I am retired, but people call me “still active.”

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 우리 학자들은 생각할 수 있는 동안 어느 정도 “계속 일할” 수 있다는 점에서 운이 좋다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: We academics are lucky in that we can to some degree “keep on working” as long as we can think.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 다행히도 나는 여전히 여러 나라에서 이따금 기조강연과 비공식 발표를 해 달라는 초대를 받고, 글도 계속 쓴다!
sentence_pairs.source_text: I am fortunate to still be invited to give occasional keynotes and informal presentations in several countries, and I still write!

entries.source_text: Time buffers and rest between engagements are essential parts of my scheduling, but I sometimes miscalculate and disappoint good people. I smiled wryly at B.F. Skinner’s comment at age 79: “If you tried to do something very serious in every waking hour, you wouldn’t last a year!” (Jennes, 1983). Do I think of finitude? Yes, but I have done that for decades. Right now, the hardest finitude thoughts are about the possibility of losing my only aunt, my most central co-biographer. She, like my father did, feels full of days. Do I worry about getting frail and in need of care? Not often. Here, my location in a Nordic welfare state makes a clear difference. Even though I have modest financial resources, I trust that I will be taken care of. My cancer experience gives me confidence. After my treatment, my oldest daughter commented, “she [I] was a patient for more than a year, but never paid a cent—and never filled out a form!”

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 일정 사이에 완충시간과 휴식을 두는 것은 내 시간계획의 필수 요소지만, 때로는 계산을 잘못해 좋은 사람들을 실망시킨다.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 치료가 끝난 뒤 큰딸은 “엄마는 1년 넘게 환자였지만 한 푼도 내지 않았고, 서류 한 장 작성하지 않았어!”라고 말했다.

entries.source_text: Moving into my great-grandfather’s 120-year-old house constituted “going home.” But I am there as a “double stranger”: I am in some ways a foreigner, and I am old. What is the best part of having entered the country of the old? Freedom! I can say no, and express what I think, without worries about long-term repercussions. I also find that children see me as more approachable. It is easier to interact, be silly, to teach and be taught by them. A teenage neighbor and I have a nice division of labor: She helps me with housework or gardening beyond my physical capacity; I help her with schoolwork and sorting out future educational options. But the greatest gift of old age is the family. I am fortunate to have two siblings and two generations of younger, constantly developing, persons—people whom I have known since they were born! I am counting weeks to summer walks with visiting children, grandchildren, and friends, picking wild flowers and berries, which will later be enjoyed around the old round table with a peaceful view of the river.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 120년 된 증조부의 집으로 이사한 것은 “집으로 돌아감”을 의미했다.

entries.source_text: Like GOH, my parents, Diann and Richard, were born during World War II. They are roughly the same age as GOH, and yet the precariousness of their early lives more closely resembles GOH’s parents. As children, they knew poverty. Their parents were born to immigrants who settled in northern Wisconsin with others of Scandinavian and German heritage. Both came from families with seven children spanning a dozen years. Both came from a small town where a nearby paper mill provided full-time work for some men, but where most men had sporadic employment away from home, farmed the land, or moved significant distance in search of opportunity.

entries.source_text: Like many children from fragile families, they would learn about interdependence and the need to rely on each other, at an early age. Older siblings were often engaged in makeshift work to help their families survive or were caring for younger siblings. At the age of 9, my mother experienced the sudden death of her father, which exacerbated their hardship. My mother’s experiences, especially, would leave her highly sensitive to social and economic inequalities. I carry in me her memories of hunger and of the deprivation she felt relative to other children. To this day, I cannot eat in the presence of someone else without offering whatever I have, and I derive much pleasure in cooking for others. At the grocery, I often purchase brands my mother used to prepare meals when I was young because these things have symbolic meaning.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 취약한 가정의 많은 아이와 마찬가지로, 두 분은 어린 나이에 상호의존성과 서로 의지해야 할 필요성을 배웠다.

entries.source_text: In the postwar era, my parents would achieve stability by taking fast paths into adulthood: They met in high school, promptly married upon graduation, and began having children. To build a more secure life, my father followed his brother and brother-in-law to southeastern Wisconsin, where the shores of Lake Michigan were peppered with factories that symbolized the promise of a better life. My dad was a machinist; my mom, a homemaker. Three sons came quickly, and a daughter followed a decade later. They worked hard, built their nest, and were happy.

entries.source_text: My parents would offer their children far more than they ever had. Their life choices and family commitments were what enabled me to experience class travel. Though the only child to do so, I would not only go to college but also receive a doctorate. This pathway has sometimes left me a stranger to the parents and siblings I love, as they do not always know how to relate to me or fully understand my life, which can make it difficult to find shared meaning. I have learned how to cross boundaries created by social class. Unlike more privileged peers, I was not socialized to be in these worlds and I have privately struggled to crack the codes of these environments in order to be successful in them. Like GOH, I have often been “the first” or “the only.”

entries.source_text: The sense of being a stranger was deepened by the stigma of being gay. I met my partner Dan as an undergraduate student. We came from similar families and towns and understood each other’s worlds. But we also left behind some systems of meaning that shaped our early development and self. We made the journey into adulthood without clear scripts related to what it meant to be gay men, let alone how to build a life as a gay couple. It was also the 1980s: a hedonistic culture, the AIDS crisis in full force, and rampant hate crimes at gay establishments. This climate only exacerbated the uncertainties we faced. And we, like many others we knew, would come to know first-hand the dark reality of homophobia in America. By the mid-1990s, when we moved from Chicago to Cleveland, we had become political activists and leaders in the LGBT community. We had created a convoy of like-minded others committed to making social change, and out of these social networks sprung family-like relationships.

entries.source_text: When we came out to our parents, we were frightened that they would reject us, and the road would, indeed, be challenging. Being gay accentuated our position as strangers to our families. We are also the only family members who have left our hometowns. The decades of geographic distance have created chasms that are sometimes difficult to bridge. Our siblings and parents have weekly and even daily interactions. They have a history of interdependence that we are not part of and will never know. As a result, we do not have the same opportunities to create shared meanings in our relationships.

entries.source_text: My desire to become a father made it difficult to come to terms with being gay, especially at a time when “gay” was incompatible with “father.” To our knowledge, we were the first gay couple to adopt children in the state of Ohio. This made us vanguards, charting unknown terrain. In the early 2000s, we had no legal recognition as a couple. The adoption was approved quietly in the chambers of a magistrate who did not want to acknowledge or draw attention to our status as gay. I would be the adoptive parent; Dan would be “Household Member 1.” Dan was kept outside the magistrate’s chambers while she discussed the fate of our children with me alone.

entries.source_text: We adopted two children, both as toddlers, a girl and then a boy. Our family composition would again deepen our experiences as strangers because we were not just men raising children; we were White men raising Black children. This has left us painfully aware of the reality of another stigma—racism—as we have crossed social borders. At the same time, our unusual family has often triggered extraordinary expressions of support, sometimes from people and in places we have least expected it.

entries.source_text: For many people, laws and legal transitions “back up” the roles that are at the core of our adult selves, such as partner and parent. In our case, laws and policies instead repeatedly reinforce our marginality by sounding clear messages of exclusion. As adoptive fathers, we were not permitted parental leave at Case Western Reserve University because leaves were only offered to mothers who had physically birthed children. Until 2015, our 30-year relationship was not recognized in federal law. Any securities that gay couples and their families might have enjoyed were a function of state-level policies and subject to changing tides at voting booths.

entries.source_text: Refugees of sorts, we have had to chase the law in order to secure basic protection—wandering in search of kinder policies. In 2006, we uprooted our family from Ohio in order to live in a state (Oregon) that would allow us to co-adopt our children. In 2014, we were allowed to marry in the state of Washington and be recognized as spouses in Oregon. Despite the fact that we are a long-lived couple, the clock to social security spousal benefits only started to tick in June 2015, with the landmark Supreme Court decision of Obergefell v. Hodges. Although this ruling should guarantee same-sex couples in all states the right to marry and have marriages recognized, it is being contested in some states. This puts families in a state of legal and social purgatory. These legal decisions affect aging because they affect rights of survivorship, inheritance tax benefits, involvement in medical care, and decision-making about end-of-life care.

entries.source_text: Our history as refugees has brought consequences for our convoys. The move to Oregon meant that we had to leave a supportive network in Cleveland, including relationships with Black families and the Black community. Given the distance, we now only see our parents and siblings once a year. Thinking about our parents’ deaths is difficult; talking about it in my family is taboo. My parents’ discomfort with death has made it difficult to discuss their finitude and to anticipate what they may need or want in their final years.

entries.source_text: Recently, I asked my parents if they judged their own aging against that of their parents. The thought had never dawned on them. Their choices and opportunities were worlds apart from their parents. And yet, my mother Diann’s aging has been precarious and not so different from her mother’s. Diann was diagnosed with diabetes and extremely high blood pressure at the age of 58, had double by-pass and carotid surgeries at the age of 60, and stays close to home for fear of being too far from medical help. Her illnesses command her attention and shape her daily decisions. Like many women, she might live with chronic illnesses for decades. My father was diagnosed with prostate cancer in his late 60s and had a few years of intense treatment. Otherwise, he is the epitome of active aging.

entries.source_text: What do my parents’ illness experiences mean for me? As they expressed, cohort changes and personal choices mean that the aging experiences of one generation are not readily applicable to another. But because aging is interpersonal, parents are our most natural personal and historical anchors and our closest models of positive or negative aging. I cannot help but engage in mental gymnastics, remembering what they were like when they were my age. I use them as a yardstick for measuring my own aging. And because I am the spitting image of my father, I literally see him when I look in the mirror!

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 부모의 질병 경험은 내게 무엇을 의미하는가?

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 부모가 말했듯 코호트 변화와 개인적 선택 때문에 한 세대의 노화 경험을 다른 세대에 그대로 적용하기는 어렵다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: As they expressed, cohort changes and personal choices mean that the aging experiences of one generation are not readily applicable to another.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 그러나 노화는 대인관계적이므로 부모는 우리의 가장 자연스러운 개인적·역사적 준거이자 긍정적 또는 부정적 노화에 관한 가장 가까운 본보기다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: But because aging is interpersonal, parents are our most natural personal and historical anchors and our closest models of positive or negative aging.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 나는 부모가 내 나이였을 때 어떤 모습이었는지 떠올리는 정신적 곡예를 하지 않을 수 없다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: I cannot help but engage in mental gymnastics, remembering what they were like when they were my age.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 부모를 내 노화를 재는 잣대로 사용한다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: I use them as a yardstick for measuring my own aging.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 그리고 나는 아버지와 판박이이므로 거울을 보면 말 그대로 아버지가 보인다!
sentence_pairs.source_text: And because I am the spitting image of my father, I literally see him when I look in the mirror!

entries.source_text: As I near the onset ages of their major illness events or diagnoses, I sense that I am entering a period of increased vulnerability. This is reinforced in exchanges with physicians, who are quick to assess my risk with my family history. As I complained of emerging problems at my annual physical—hair loss, a thicker waistline, evening fatigue, and losing my edge in sprinting matches with my preteen son—the doctor cynically replied, “Well, what do you expect at your age?!” But my health and my self are more than my genes and my age! My changing body nevertheless affects how I see myself and how others see me. Recently, my son repeatedly noted in looking at the daily newspaper that I resembled one man or another in a photo. It took a dozen such comments for me to realize that what we all had in common was the same diminishing hairline! In a society that places a premium on youthfulness, my aging body leaves me with a palpable new sense that I am becoming invisible in public spaces.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 부모가 주요 질병을 겪거나 진단받은 나이에 가까워질수록 나는 취약성이 높아지는 시기에 들어선다는 느낌을 받는다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: As I near the onset ages of their major illness events or diagnoses, I sense that I am entering a period of increased vulnerability.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 가족력으로 내 위험을 재빨리 평가하는 의사들과의 대화는 이러한 느낌을 강화한다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: This is reinforced in exchanges with physicians, who are quick to assess my risk with my family history.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 연례 건강검진에서 탈모, 굵어진 허리, 저녁의 피로, 사춘기 직전 아들과 단거리 달리기 시합을 할 때 예전의 기량을 잃는 문제를 호소하자 의사는 냉소적으로 “글쎄요, 그 나이에 뭘 기대하십니까?!”라고 답했다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: As I complained of emerging problems at my annual physical—hair loss, a thicker waistline, evening fatigue, and losing my edge in sprinting matches with my preteen son—the doctor cynically replied, “Well, what do you expect at your age?!”

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 그러나 내 건강과 자아는 유전자와 나이 그 이상이다!
sentence_pairs.source_text: But my health and my self are more than my genes and my age!

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 그럼에도 변화하는 내 몸은 내가 나 자신을 보는 방식과 타인이 나를 보는 방식에 영향을 미친다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: My changing body nevertheless affects how I see myself and how others see me.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 최근 아들은 일간신문을 보면서 사진 속 이 남자 또는 저 남자와 내가 닮았다고 거듭 말했다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: Recently, my son repeatedly noted in looking at the daily newspaper that I resembled one man or another in a photo.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 그런 말을 열두 번쯤 듣고서야 나는 우리 모두의 공통점이 똑같이 뒤로 물러난 헤어라인이라는 사실을 깨달았다!
sentence_pairs.source_text: It took a dozen such comments for me to realize that what we all had in common was the same diminishing hairline!

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 젊음을 중시하는 사회에서 나이 들어가는 몸은 내가 공적 공간에서 보이지 않는 존재가 되어간다는 생생하고 새로운 감각을 남긴다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: In a society that places a premium on youthfulness, my aging body leaves me with a palpable new sense that I am becoming invisible in public spaces.

entries.source_text: The illness experiences of older consociates also enter my consciousness, even though there is no genetic connection. When GOH was diagnosed with cancer over two decades ago, it left me with a shattered sense of predictability too. I am now the age she was then, and that memory is alive in my mind. My life could come undone just as quickly and unexpectedly, with effects spreading like contagion through my social relationships.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 유전적 연관이 전혀 없는데도 나이 든 생활세계 동료들의 질병 경험 역시 내 의식 속으로 들어온다. 20여 년 전 GOH가 암 진단을 받았을 때, 내 예측가능성에 대한 감각도 산산이 부서졌다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: The illness experiences of older consociates also enter my consciousness, even though there is no genetic connection. When GOH was diagnosed with cancer over two decades ago, it left me with a shattered sense of predictability too.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 이제 나는 당시 그녀의 나이가 되었고, 그 기억은 내 마음속에 생생하다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: I am now the age she was then, and that memory is alive in my mind.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 내 삶도 그처럼 빠르고 예기치 않게 무너질 수 있으며, 그 영향은 전염병처럼 사회적 관계를 통해 퍼져 나갈 수 있다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: My life could come undone just as quickly and unexpectedly, with effects spreading like contagion through my social relationships.

entries.source_text: Interpersonal experiences with illness and death have heightened my awareness of life’s finitude. I am acutely aware that a relationship is running out of time, that time gotten is a kind of “grace time,” and that death may take it away before I am ready. For men especially, death is the enemy lurking around the corner. Men, more than women, drop dead without warning—like a special friend of my age out for a daily jog or the man standing near me at the airport carousel waiting for his luggage.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 질병과 죽음을 둘러싼 대인관계 경험은 삶의 유한성에 대한 내 인식을 높였다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: Interpersonal experiences with illness and death have heightened my awareness of life’s finitude.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 나는 관계에 남은 시간이 줄어들고 있으며, 얻은 시간이 일종의 “은총의 시간”이고, 내가 준비되기 전에 죽음이 그것을 앗아갈 수 있음을 절실히 인식한다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: I am acutely aware that a relationship is running out of time, that time gotten is a kind of “grace time,” and that death may take it away before I am ready.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 특히 남성에게 죽음은 모퉁이에 숨어 있는 적이다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: For men especially, death is the enemy lurking around the corner.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 남성은 여성보다 아무 경고 없이 돌연사하는 일이 더 많다. 매일 조깅하러 나갔던 나와 같은 나이의 각별한 친구나, 공항 수하물 회전대에서 짐을 기다리며 내 곁에 서 있던 남성처럼 말이다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: Men, more than women, drop dead without warning—like a special friend of my age out for a daily jog or the man standing near me at the airport carousel waiting for his luggage.

entries.source_text: Now that I am situated squarely in middle age, I think much more about time left. I worry about the fact that eventually, Dan or I will become a widower and our children will be orphaned. We need each other; our children need us. In the U.S. context, we have cared for children and managed family life in ways that mothers, not fathers, normally do. We have cultivated a capacity for what Jung (1930) called “tender feelings” before most men suddenly discover them at midlife. My father was a vanguard in this regard: not only a provider but also highly involved in domestic roles and actively engaged with his children. He is a role model for me.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 이제 중년의 한가운데에 확실히 자리한 나는 남은 시간을 훨씬 더 많이 생각한다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: Now that I am situated squarely in middle age, I think much more about time left.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 언젠가 Dan과 나 중 한 사람이 홀아비가 되고 아이들이 부모를 잃게 된다는 사실이 걱정스럽다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: I worry about the fact that eventually, Dan or I will become a widower and our children will be orphaned.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 우리는 서로가 필요하고, 아이들은 우리가 필요하다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: We need each other; our children need us.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 미국의 맥락에서 우리는 보통 아버지가 아니라 어머니가 하는 방식으로 아이를 돌보고 가족생활을 운영해 왔다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: In the U.S. context, we have cared for children and managed family life in ways that mothers, not fathers, normally do.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 우리는 대부분의 남성이 중년에 갑자기 발견하는, Jung(1930)이 “다정한 감정”이라고 부른 능력을 일찍부터 길렀다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: We have cultivated a capacity for what Jung (1930) called “tender feelings” before most men suddenly discover them at midlife.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 이 점에서 아버지는 선구자였다. 그는 생계부양자였을 뿐 아니라 가사역할에도 깊이 참여하고 자녀와 적극적으로 관계 맺었다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: My father was a vanguard in this regard: not only a provider but also highly involved in domestic roles and actively engaged with his children.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 아버지는 나의 역할모델이다.

entries.source_text: Our parenting experiences may serve us well in old age. As caretakers and kin-keepers, we will be embedded in wider and deeper relationships than most old men—but our emotional losses will likely be greater for it. In a strange way, those losses, and the agism and invisibility that can accompany later life, may be easier because we have been subject to stigma and prejudice earlier in our lives, and we have had to develop a repertoire of strategies to cope with it.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 양육 경험은 노년에 우리에게 도움이 될 수 있다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: Our parenting experiences may serve us well in old age.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 돌봄제공자이자 친족관계 유지자로서 우리는 대부분의 노년 남성보다 더 넓고 깊은 관계 속에 놓일 것이지만, 그 때문에 정서적 상실도 더 클 가능성이 있다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: As caretakers and kin-keepers, we will be embedded in wider and deeper relationships than most old men—but our emotional losses will likely be greater for it.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 이상하게도 그러한 상실과 노년기에 동반될 수 있는 연령주의 및 비가시성은 오히려 견디기 쉬울지 모른다. 우리는 삶의 이른 시기에 낙인과 편견의 대상이었고, 이에 대처할 전략의 레퍼토리를 개발해야 했기 때문이다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: In a strange way, those losses, and the agism and invisibility that can accompany later life, may be easier because we have been subject to stigma and prejudice earlier in our lives, and we have had to develop a repertoire of strategies to cope with it.

entries.source_text: Gay couples and families challenge many assumptions in theories and models about gendered care and caregiving, whether men caring for their male spouses or children caring for gay parents. However, aging policies and programs in the United States will not care for me in the way those in Norway will care for GOH. The neoliberal ethos of the American welfare state does not foster independence as much as it assumes interdependence—and therefore brings stark interpersonal ramifications. It provides a much shallower reservoir of formal care and places the responsibility of managing aging in the private hands of individuals and their families.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 남성이 남성 배우자를 돌보거나 자녀가 게이 부모를 돌보는 경우를 비롯해, 게이 커플과 가족은 젠더화된 돌봄 및 돌봄제공에 관한 이론과 모형의 여러 가정에 도전한다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: Gay couples and families challenge many assumptions in theories and models about gendered care and caregiving, whether men caring for their male spouses or children caring for gay parents.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 그러나 미국의 노화정책과 프로그램은 노르웨이의 제도가 GOH를 돌보는 방식으로 나를 돌보지 않을 것이다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: However, aging policies and programs in the United States will not care for me in the way those in Norway will care for GOH.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 미국 복지국가의 신자유주의적 기풍은 독립성을 길러내기보다 상호의존성을 전제하며, 그 때문에 뚜렷한 대인관계적 파장을 낳는다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: The neoliberal ethos of the American welfare state does not foster independence as much as it assumes interdependence—and therefore brings stark interpersonal ramifications.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 미국 복지국가는 공식적 돌봄의 저수지를 훨씬 얕게 제공하고 노화를 관리할 책임을 개인과 가족의 사적 손에 맡긴다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: It provides a much shallower reservoir of formal care and places the responsibility of managing aging in the private hands of individuals and their families.

entries.source_text: Our stories show how history leaves individuals with scars, vulnerabilities, and strengths, which in turn affect interpersonal ties. The personal accounts also illustrate how the impact of history transcends family generations. GOH’s views of precariousness and unpredictability reflect her mother’s historical experiences, which in turn, were shaped by the grandparental generation. Indeed, RAS’s views on the same issues have even been influenced by Bertha—through GOH! Consciously or not, we carry and transmit historical influences faced by our parents. It is not just our own cohort that lurs as a force in our lives, but also the cohorts of people who are close to us, especially in the family. This phenomenon is for the most part disregarded in the cohort literature. Our stories also illustrate that, in considering cohorts and periods, attention to herstory alongside history is essential.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 우리의 이야기는 역사가 개인에게 상처, 취약성, 강점을 남기고, 이것들이 다시 대인관계 유대에 영향을 미치는 방식을 보여준다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: Our stories show how history leaves individuals with scars, vulnerabilities, and strengths, which in turn affect interpersonal ties.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 또한 개인적 기록은 역사의 영향이 가족 세대를 넘어서는 방식을 보여준다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: The personal accounts also illustrate how the impact of history transcends family generations.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 불안정성과 예측불가능성에 대한 GOH의 관점은 어머니의 역사적 경험을 반영하며, 그 경험은 다시 조부모 세대에 의해 형성되었다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: GOH’s views of precariousness and unpredictability reflect her mother’s historical experiences, which in turn, were shaped by the grandparental generation.

sentence_pairs.source_text: Indeed, RAS’s views on the same issues have even been influenced by Bertha—through GOH!

sentence_pairs.source_text: Consciously or not, we carry and transmit historical influences faced by our parents.

entries.source_text: Between the starting points of GOH’s parents’ lives and those of RAS’s parents, the demographic transition—sometimes called a revolution—made lives longer and more predictable. In aging societies finitude has, to a dramatic degree, become linked to old age. In this process, the “denial of death” (Becker, 1973) has become stronger.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: GOH 부모의 삶이 출발한 시점과 RAS 부모의 삶이 출발한 시점 사이에, 때로 혁명이라고 불리는 인구학적 전환이 일어나 삶은 더 길고 예측 가능해졌다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: Between the starting points of GOH’s parents’ lives and those of RAS’s parents, the demographic transition—sometimes called a revolution—made lives longer and more predictable.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 고령사회에서는 유한성이 극적인 정도로 노년과 연결되었다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: In aging societies finitude has, to a dramatic degree, become linked to old age.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 이 과정에서 “죽음의 부정”(Becker, 1973)은 더욱 강해졌다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: In this process, the “denial of death” (Becker, 1973) has become stronger.

entries.source_text: The historical shift from the risk of death being “ageless” to it being primarily linked to old age becomes personal reality through our mothers. Bertha exemplifies “prerevolutionary” life, focused on precariousness and unpredictability. To her, death was omnipresent, independently of age. Diann is an example of the other side of the watershed in feeling such discomfort with the end of life. Because of GOH’s early years in the war and experience with critical illness, she is more like her mother than her peer Diann in views on life, death, and precariousness. RAS belongs to a cohort from the other side of the demographic divide, but as a middle-aged man sees precariousness quite differently from his mother. This could also be because he has seen close consociates face serious illness, even death, and experienced grave uncertainties due to legal restrictions, prejudice, and stigma. His growing sense of finitude is part of what Neugarten (1968) called the “awareness of middle age.” She observed that between the ages of 40 and 60 years, individuals start thinking in terms of time left rather than time lived. The ability to make this shift itself rests on having a relatively long and predictable life expectancy.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 죽음의 위험이 “나이를 가리지 않던” 상태에서 주로 노년과 연결되는 상태로 바뀐 역사적 전환은 우리의 어머니들을 통해 개인적 현실이 된다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: The historical shift from the risk of death being “ageless” to it being primarily linked to old age becomes personal reality through our mothers.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: Bertha는 불안정성과 예측불가능성에 초점을 둔 “혁명 이전”의 삶을 보여준다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: Bertha exemplifies “prerevolutionary” life, focused on precariousness and unpredictability.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 그녀에게 죽음은 나이와 무관하게 어디에나 존재했다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: To her, death was omnipresent, independently of age.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: Diann은 생의 끝에 그토록 불편함을 느낀다는 점에서 분수령의 반대편을 보여주는 사례다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: Diann is an example of the other side of the watershed in feeling such discomfort with the end of life.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: GOH는 전쟁 속에서 보낸 어린 시절과 중병 경험 때문에 삶, 죽음, 불안정성에 관한 관점에서 또래인 Diann보다 자신의 어머니와 더 비슷하다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: Because of GOH’s early years in the war and experience with critical illness, she is more like her mother than her peer Diann in views on life, death, and precariousness.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: RAS는 인구학적 분할선 반대편의 코호트에 속하지만, 중년 남성으로서 불안정성을 어머니와는 상당히 다르게 본다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: RAS belongs to a cohort from the other side of the demographic divide, but as a middle-aged man sees precariousness quite differently from his mother.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 이는 그가 가까운 생활세계의 동료들이 중병, 심지어 죽음에 직면하는 모습을 보았고 법적 제약, 편견, 낙인으로 인한 심각한 불확실성을 경험했기 때문일 수도 있다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: This could also be because he has seen close consociates face serious illness, even death, and experienced grave uncertainties due to legal restrictions, prejudice, and stigma.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 커져가는 그의 유한성 감각은 Neugarten(1968)이 “중년의 인식”이라고 부른 것의 일부다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: His growing sense of finitude is part of what Neugarten (1968) called the “awareness of middle age.”

sentence_pairs.ko_text: Neugarten은 40세에서 60세 사이에 사람들이 살아온 시간이 아니라 남은 시간의 관점에서 생각하기 시작한다고 관찰했다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: She observed that between the ages of 40 and 60 years, individuals start thinking in terms of time left rather than time lived.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 이러한 전환을 할 수 있는 능력 자체가 비교적 길고 예측 가능한 기대수명을 전제로 한다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: The ability to make this shift itself rests on having a relatively long and predictable life expectancy.

entries.source_text: Since Neugarten’s essay, life expectancies have increased and actuarial patterns have become even more predictable. In 1976, Cain put forward a revolutionary proposal that age-based entitlements be given on the basis of a demographic category’s remaining life expectancy. Recently, demographers and policy makers have suggested that time left be used as the basis of certain rights, such as pension (e.g., Vaupel, 2010). If pension policies are changed—a reform that is part of policy discussions in several countries—will this bring altered views of finitude?

sentence_pairs.ko_text: Neugarten의 논고가 나온 뒤 기대수명은 늘었고 보험계리적 양상은 한층 더 예측 가능해졌다. 1976년 Cain은 연령을 기준으로 부여되는 수급권을 인구집단 범주의 잔여 기대수명을 기준으로 부여하자는 혁명적인 제안을 내놓았다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: Since Neugarten’s essay, life expectancies have increased and actuarial patterns have become even more predictable. In 1976, Cain put forward a revolutionary proposal that age-based entitlements be given on the basis of a demographic category’s remaining life expectancy.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 최근 인구학자와 정책입안자는 남은 시간을 연금 같은 특정 권리의 근거로 삼자고 제안했다(예: Vaupel, 2010).
sentence_pairs.source_text: Recently, demographers and policy makers have suggested that time left be used as the basis of certain rights, such as pension (e.g., Vaupel, 2010).

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 여러 나라의 정책 논의에 포함된 개혁으로서 연금정책이 바뀐다면, 이는 유한성에 관한 관점의 변화를 가져올까?
sentence_pairs.source_text: If pension policies are changed—a reform that is part of policy discussions in several countries—will this bring altered views of finitude?

entries.source_text: Diann also exemplifies a second watershed: the epidemiological transition. In the 20th century, causes of death shifted from infectious disease to lifestyle-related illnesses. With this shift, gender differences in mortality and morbidity widened. Men are more likely to die from acute illness; aging women have more chronic conditions, such as Type 2 diabetes and arthritis. An English saying sums it up: “Women are sicker; men die quicker.” It is also important to keep in mind that, starting in teenage years, women are more used to living “at the will of the body” (Frank, 1991) due to menstrual cycles, pregnancies, births, and menopause. As a result of demographic change, women’s convoys are more characterized by co-longevity and relationships of long duration than is the case for men. This gives old women more available consociates and co-biographers.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: Diann은 두 번째 분수령인 역학적 전환도 보여준다. 20세기에는 사망원인이 감염병에서 생활습관 관련 질환으로 이동했다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: Diann also exemplifies a second watershed: the epidemiological transition. In the 20th century, causes of death shifted from infectious disease to lifestyle-related illnesses.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 이 변화와 함께 사망률과 유병률의 젠더 차이가 벌어졌다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: With this shift, gender differences in mortality and morbidity widened.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 남성은 급성질환으로 사망할 가능성이 더 크고, 나이 든 여성은 제2형 당뇨병과 관절염 같은 만성질환을 더 많이 지닌다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: Men are more likely to die from acute illness; aging women have more chronic conditions, such as Type 2 diabetes and arthritis.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 영어 속담은 이를 “여성은 더 아프고, 남성은 더 빨리 죽는다”라고 요약한다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: An English saying sums it up: “Women are sicker; men die quicker.”

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 또한 여성은 월경주기, 임신, 출산, 폐경 때문에 청소년기부터 “몸의 의지대로”(Frank, 1991) 사는 데 더 익숙하다는 점을 염두에 두어야 한다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: It is also important to keep in mind that, starting in teenage years, women are more used to living “at the will of the body” (Frank, 1991) due to menstrual cycles, pregnancies, births, and menopause.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 인구학적 변화의 결과로 여성의 관계망은 남성보다 동시 장수와 오래 지속되는 관계의 특성을 더 강하게 띤다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: As a result of demographic change, women’s convoys are more characterized by co-longevity and relationships of long duration than is the case for men.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 이 때문에 노년 여성에게는 생활세계의 동료와 공동 전기작가가 더 많이 남아 있다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: This gives old women more available consociates and co-biographers.

entries.source_text: Social change does not just “happen”—it is often deliberately created. Both of us have experienced making and living social change, being “the first” or “the only” in choosing new life course options. For GOH, such experiences are closely linked to changes in gender roles. Women, more than men, have used new educational opportunities and have greater attainment in high school and beyond.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 사회변화는 그저 “일어나는” 것이 아니라 흔히 의도적으로 만들어진다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: Social change does not just “happen”—it is often deliberately created.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 우리 두 사람 모두 새로운 생애과정 선택지를 택한 “최초” 또는 “유일한 사람”이 되어 사회변화를 만들고 살아낸 경험이 있다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: Both of us have experienced making and living social change, being “the first” or “the only” in choosing new life course options.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: GOH에게 그러한 경험은 젠더역할의 변화와 밀접하게 연결되어 있다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: For GOH, such experiences are closely linked to changes in gender roles.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 여성은 남성보다 새로운 교육기회를 더 많이 활용했으며 고등학교와 그 이상의 교육단계에서 더 높은 학업성취를 보인다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: Women, more than men, have used new educational opportunities and have greater attainment in high school and beyond.

entries.source_text: RAS has also been part of an educational vanguard within the community where he grew up, but his strongest experiences come from being part of a gay married couple and becoming an adoptive parent. He partnered in an era when this choice was even more difficult than today. A gay couple adopting children, let alone a White couple adopting Black children, was unthinkable a few decades ago. Being vanguards makes building and maintaining support convoys difficult, but essential. Will it also help us cope with aging, given that we have built strategies for resilience in the face of hardship and stigma?

sentence_pairs.ko_text: RAS 역시 자신이 성장한 공동체 안에서 교육의 선구자 집단에 속했지만, 그의 가장 강렬한 경험은 결혼한 게이 커플의 일원이 되고 입양부모가 된 데서 나온다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: RAS has also been part of an educational vanguard within the community where he grew up, but his strongest experiences come from being part of a gay married couple and becoming an adoptive parent.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 그는 이러한 선택이 오늘날보다 훨씬 더 어려웠던 시대에 파트너 관계를 맺었다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: He partnered in an era when this choice was even more difficult than today.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 게이 커플이 아이를 입양하는 것, 더구나 백인 커플이 흑인 아이를 입양하는 것은 불과 몇십 년 전만 해도 상상할 수 없었다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: A gay couple adopting children, let alone a White couple adopting Black children, was unthinkable a few decades ago.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 선구자가 되면 지원 관계망을 구축하고 유지하기가 어렵지만, 그러한 관계망은 반드시 필요하다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: Being vanguards makes building and maintaining support convoys difficult, but essential.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 역경과 낙인에 맞서 회복탄력성을 발휘할 전략을 구축해 왔다는 점을 고려하면, 선구자였던 경험은 노화에 대처하는 데도 도움이 될까?
sentence_pairs.source_text: Will it also help us cope with aging, given that we have built strategies for resilience in the face of hardship and stigma?

entries.source_text: RAS’s vanguard family is linked to a more general phenomenon: men’s increasing engagement in parenting. It is possible that this shift, in which the Nordic countries have been pioneers, may signal a sea change for men in late life. Will new fathers, who created and sustained strong ties to children, have a better old age than earlier cohorts of men? Will they have built stronger convoys?

sentence_pairs.ko_text: RAS의 선구적인 가족은 남성의 양육 참여 증가라는 더 일반적인 현상과 연결되어 있다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: RAS’s vanguard family is linked to a more general phenomenon: men’s increasing engagement in parenting.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 북유럽 국가들이 앞장선 이러한 변화는 노년기 남성에게 거대한 변화를 알리는 신호일 수 있다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: It is possible that this shift, in which the Nordic countries have been pioneers, may signal a sea change for men in late life.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 자녀와 강한 유대를 만들고 유지한 새로운 세대의 아버지들은 이전 코호트의 남성보다 더 나은 노년을 보낼까?
sentence_pairs.source_text: Will new fathers, who created and sustained strong ties to children, have a better old age than earlier cohorts of men?

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 그들은 더 강한 관계망을 구축했을까?
sentence_pairs.source_text: Will they have built stronger convoys?

entries.source_text: The life course perspective sees individual lives are interwoven in webs of interdependence, especially in the family (for illustrations, see Settersten, 2015). In our stories, we placed ourselves in such a fabric, spanning several generations. Interdependence is not only a matter of how individual circumstances are connected, but how societal conditions affect lives through relationships (Elder, 1974). In the family realm, interdependence is also structured through laws and policies (Hagestad & Dykstra, 2016). The complex interactions of interdependent rights and obligations are illustrated in Norwegian policies regarding care leaves. The law provides a given duration of paid leave to care for sick family members. However, when the illness period exceeds the stipulated length of leave, caregivers may risk loss of full pension rights because they will not meet the duration requirements for continuous paid employment. Laws and policies may also block interdependence, as when grandparents are not granted the right to raise grandchildren.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 생애과정 관점은 개인의 삶이 특히 가족 안에서 상호의존성의 그물로 얽혀 있다고 본다(사례는 Settersten, 2015 참조).
sentence_pairs.source_text: The life course perspective sees individual lives are interwoven in webs of interdependence, especially in the family (for illustrations, see Settersten, 2015).

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 우리의 이야기에서 우리는 여러 세대에 걸친 그러한 직물 안에 자신을 놓았다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: In our stories, we placed ourselves in such a fabric, spanning several generations.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 상호의존성은 개인의 상황들이 어떻게 연결되는가뿐 아니라 사회적 조건이 관계를 통해 삶에 어떻게 영향을 미치는가의 문제이기도 하다(Elder, 1974).
sentence_pairs.source_text: Interdependence is not only a matter of how individual circumstances are connected, but how societal conditions affect lives through relationships (Elder, 1974).

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 가족 영역의 상호의존성은 법과 정책을 통해 구조화되기도 한다(Hagestad & Dykstra, 2016).
sentence_pairs.source_text: In the family realm, interdependence is also structured through laws and policies (Hagestad & Dykstra, 2016).

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 상호의존적 권리와 의무 사이의 복잡한 상호작용은 가족돌봄휴가에 관한 노르웨이 정책에서 드러난다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: The complex interactions of interdependent rights and obligations are illustrated in Norwegian policies regarding care leaves.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 법은 아픈 가족을 돌볼 수 있도록 일정 기간의 유급휴가를 보장한다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: The law provides a given duration of paid leave to care for sick family members.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 그러나 질병 기간이 규정된 휴가기간을 넘으면 돌봄제공자는 계속 유급고용을 유지해야 한다는 기간 요건을 충족하지 못해 완전한 연금권을 잃을 위험이 있다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: However, when the illness period exceeds the stipulated length of leave, caregivers may risk loss of full pension rights because they will not meet the duration requirements for continuous paid employment.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 조부모에게 손주를 양육할 권리를 부여하지 않는 경우처럼, 법과 정책은 상호의존성을 가로막기도 한다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: Laws and policies may also block interdependence, as when grandparents are not granted the right to raise grandchildren.

entries.source_text: On a personal level, if individuals have supportive and reliable relationships, interdependence can provide stability and continuity in later life, but it can also bring risks, change, and unpredictability. We are not only at the will of our own bodies but also the functioning of others. Relationships can make aging a highly contingent enterprise. It is also important not to limit considerations of interdependence to the here and now. Norms of reciprocity may span long periods: You helped me out 50 years ago, so now it is my turn to help you live with the new precariousness of aging.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 개인적 수준에서 지지적이고 신뢰할 수 있는 관계가 있다면 상호의존성은 노년기에 안정성과 연속성을 제공할 수 있지만, 위험과 변화, 예측불가능성을 가져올 수도 있다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: On a personal level, if individuals have supportive and reliable relationships, interdependence can provide stability and continuity in later life, but it can also bring risks, change, and unpredictability.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 우리는 자기 몸의 의지뿐 아니라 타인의 기능에도 좌우된다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: We are not only at the will of our own bodies but also the functioning of others.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 관계는 노화를 우연적 조건에 크게 좌우되는 일로 만들 수 있다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: Relationships can make aging a highly contingent enterprise.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 또한 상호의존성을 지금 이 순간에만 국한해 고려하지 않는 것이 중요하다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: It is also important not to limit considerations of interdependence to the here and now.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 호혜성 규범은 긴 시간에 걸쳐 작동할 수 있다. 당신이 50년 전에 나를 도왔으니 이제 노화가 가져온 새로운 불안정성을 안고 살아가도록 내가 당신을 도울 차례라는 식이다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: Norms of reciprocity may span long periods: You helped me out 50 years ago, so now it is my turn to help you live with the new precariousness of aging.

entries.source_text: There is an extensive literature on gender differences in patterns of interdependence. Moen (2001) argues that women have a “contingency orientation” an attitude of “it depends.” GOH’s mother said, “if we live.” Today, many women, especially in middle generations, say, “if everyone stays healthy.” Because women live longer than men, and have lifetimes of stronger investments in relationships, they also have a more complex web of contingencies.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 상호의존성 양상의 젠더 차이에 관해서는 방대한 문헌이 있다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: There is an extensive literature on gender differences in patterns of interdependence.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: Moen(2001)은 여성에게 “상황의존적 지향”, 곧 “상황에 달려 있다”는 태도가 있다고 주장한다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: Moen (2001) argues that women have a “contingency orientation” an attitude of “it depends.”

sentence_pairs.ko_text: GOH의 어머니는 “우리가 살아 있다면”이라고 말했다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: GOH’s mother said, “if we live.”

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 오늘날 많은 여성, 특히 중간 세대의 여성은 “모두 건강하다면”이라고 말한다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: Today, many women, especially in middle generations, say, “if everyone stays healthy.”

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 여성은 남성보다 오래 살고 평생 관계에 더 많이 투자해 왔기 때문에 더 복잡한 조건의 그물을 지니기도 한다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: Because women live longer than men, and have lifetimes of stronger investments in relationships, they also have a more complex web of contingencies.

entries.source_text: In our view, interdependence of lives is the best example of how we cannot talk about personal aging without talking about interpersonal ties. A person who is not embedded in a fabric of interdependent lives might face the most naked forms of precariousness.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 우리가 보기에 삶의 상호의존성은 대인관계 유대를 말하지 않고 개인의 노화를 말할 수 없는 이유를 가장 잘 보여주는 사례다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: In our view, interdependence of lives is the best example of how we cannot talk about personal aging without talking about interpersonal ties.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 상호의존적 삶의 직물에 자리 잡지 못한 사람은 가장 적나라한 형태의 불안정성에 직면할 수 있다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: A person who is not embedded in a fabric of interdependent lives might face the most naked forms of precariousness.

entries.source_text: Old age is a time when many people face unpredictability and uncertainty. Experiences hinge on many ifs: if we have each other, if we live, if we have our health. Encounters with illness and disability make planning difficult for an increasingly uncertain future. The precariousness of contemporary old age is, in the end, much like the precariousness earlier generations experienced as a natural part of the whole life span. A central aspect of this experience is living with a body that we, to some degree, do not recognize in images presented by physical or social mirrors—they do not match our sense of self.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 노년은 많은 사람이 예측불가능성과 불확실성에 직면하는 시기다.
sentence_pairs.source_text: Old age is a time when many people face unpredictability and uncertainty.

sentence_pairs.source_text: Experiences hinge on many ifs: if we have each other, if we live, if we have our health.

entries.source_text: Some of these changes have less to do with physical functioning than with cultural meanings. Here, there are distinct gender contrasts, as looks have traditionally been at the core of women’s “presentation of self.” Powell Bell (1970) and Sontag (1972) both wrote about the “double standard of aging”: Physical signs of aging make men look distinguished and women look over the hill. Although the “double standard” disadvantages women, aging can also bring a loss of male attractiveness, as culturally defined. Physical frailty may be harder for men, because they place a premium on strength and independence. GOH’s father is an example of an older man who was ready to quit, once his body had clear limitations. entries.source_text: As GOH noted in her story, reduced functioning brings the danger of either/or thinking, especially once an individual has been labeled a “patient” or “disabled.” Being a patient becomes a dominant role—a central lens through which we see ourselves and through which others see us. Dichotomous thinking threatens the potential for social participation and contribution—a foundation for a sense of dignity and value. It also deprives society of human resources. It is worth noting that WHO for many years has urged us to not see disability solely as a personal characteristic, but as a relation between individual capacity and environmental demands. In an extensive report on disability (WHO, 2011), the organization explicitly warns against dichotomous thinking.

entries.source_text: Our stories show that we have been strangers, invisible, and faced stigma before becoming old. We have argued that these experiences have in some ways given us a preview into what it is like to be old, a preparation for the precariousness of later life. As aging individuals try to prepare for what lies ahead, honest personal accounts from gerontologists are important. We need to talk about us rather than them, avoiding a dangerous practice of “othering,” which reproduces stigma and agism. By participating in two distinct conversations—one public, one private—gerontologists create a type of “false consciousness” about growing old. Up to now, few have dared to make their private stories public. Gerontological scholars must not be part of a denial process by refusing to be honest about what aging does to the body, or by not acknowledging finitude. In 2012, the EU declared an “International Year of Active Aging and Solidarity between Generations.” Many old people felt that the “active” part of the theme received too much attention and found it discouraging. In their view, it promoted unrealistic expectations. An old Norwegian commented: “It sounds like in order to be active, you bike to a full-time job, and on weekends you climb mountains.”

entries.source_text: Our stories revealed an often invisible truth: Personal aging is tangled up in history, and history carries different footprints for men and women. Contrasts in historical circumstances entail dissimilar opportunities for building and maintaining relationships. Our examples also illustrate how our lives are shaped by historical experiences of significant others, such as parents and grandparents. In conducting research and meeting students and patients, gerontologists and geriatricians must be mindful of historical impact on intergenerational webs that shaped the lives of men and women.

sentence_pairs.ko_text: 우리의 이야기는 흔히 보이지 않는 진실을 드러냈다. 개인의 노화는 역사와 뒤얽혀 있으며, 역사는 남성과 여성에게 서로 다른 발자국을 남긴다.

entries.source_text: Being aware of history not only means looking backwards, it also means looking forward. The future of aging is already here. It can be projected for cohorts who are in middle age and outlined for young adults, youth, and children. Gerontologists must begin to map how the aging of future cohorts presents new challenges and options for society. In other words, we need to engage in what Cain (2003) called anticipatory gerontology. Such efforts include projecting how demographic, policy, and cultural changes will affect the interpersonal worlds of aging men and women, and their options for building and maintaining social ties.

entries.source_text: Relationships give aging its contours and content. Biographies are created in exchanges with co-biographers. We use others, and also serve others, as social mirrors. The experience of co-writing this essay has further intensified our awareness of such realities. In the end, our individual and joint stories illustrate that aging is more than personal—it is interpersonal!
